issue.body:
## Description

Enabling `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel` in any multi-process deployment (e.g. JAX with one process per GPU) crashes at the first ragged-all-to-all with `RET_CHECK failure ... peer_access_enabled ... Peer access must be enabled`.

## Context

We are benchmarking expert-parallel MoE training on GB200 NVL72 (4 hosts × 4 GPUs, one NVLink domain), using JAX with the standard one process per GPU. The MoE dispatch/combine steps use `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all`, and the default one-shot path is our current throughput bottleneck, so we want to evaluate the device-initiated kernel from #46116 — whose LSA lane targets exactly this topology (NCCL reports the clique as a single LSA domain, `lsa_size: 16`). Every multi-process configuration we tried crashes at the same check; single-process runs pass it and compute correct results (we verified 500 random ragged cases bitwise on 4 GPUs).

## Minimal repro

Verified on one GB200 node (4 GPUs, 4 processes) with jax/jaxlib/plugin/pjrt nightly `0.11.1.dev20260809`, CUDA 13, NCCL 2.30.7. The failing check compares process count against clique size before probing hardware, so we expect this to reproduce on any multi-GPU host:

```python
# repro.py — run one copy per GPU:
#   export XLA_FLAGS='--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true \
#     --xla_gpu_experimental_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers=true \
#     --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall'
#   for i in 0 1 2 3; do CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=$i python repro.py $i & done; wait
import sys
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, numpy as np
from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P

jax.distributed.initialize("127.0.0.1:12345", num_processes=4, process_id=int(sys.argv[1]))
n = jax.device_count()
mesh = Mesh(np.array(jax.devices()), ("x",))

def f(operand, output):
    i = jax.lax.axis_index("x").astype(jnp.int64)
    in_off = jnp.arange(n, dtype=jnp.int64)       # send row j to peer j
    sizes = jnp.ones(n, dtype=jnp.int64)
    out_off = jnp.full((n,), i, dtype=jnp.int64)  # land at receiver row = sender index
    recv = jnp.ones(n, dtype=jnp.int64)
    return jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all(operand, output, in_off, sizes, out_off, recv, axis_name="x")

operand = jnp.arange(n * 32, dtype=jnp.bfloat16).reshape(n * 8, 4)
output = jnp.zeros((n * 8, 4), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)
result = jax.jit(jax.shard_map(f, mesh=mesh, in_specs=(P("x"), P("x")), out_specs=P("x")))(operand, output)
jax.block_until_ready(result)
print(f"process {jax.process_index()}: ok", flush=True)
```

## Actual behavior

Every process crashes at the first ragged-all-to-all (verified on 4×GB200, one process per GPU; also fails identically at 4 hosts × 16 processes):

```
E0812 18:02:19.182677 status_macros.cc:58] INTERNAL: RET_CHECK failure
(external/xla/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc:943)
peer_access_enabled RaggedAllToAllThunk: Peer access must be enabled.
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: INTERNAL: RET_CHECK failure
(external/xla/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc:943)
peer_access_enabled RaggedAllToAllThunk: Peer access must be enabled.
[executable_name='jit_f']
```

The identical script with `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel` removed (other flags unchanged) completes on all processes.

## Expected behavior

The device kernel should run: its address plumbing is NCCL symmetric windows, which work cross-process.

## Root-cause hypothesis

[`EnablePeerAccess`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/7c3dd1936addd297d7c6fa46f6183986fc4160c3/xla/backends/gpu/collectives/gpu_cliques.cc#L323-L327) returns false whenever `key.devices().size() != ranks.size()` — the global clique vs the participants local to one process — so the [RET_CHECK](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/7c3dd1936addd297d7c6fa46f6183986fc4160c3/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc#L941-L944) is unsatisfiable for any multi-process clique, even though the kernel addresses peers only through `ncclGetLocalPointer`/`ncclGetLsaPointer` on registered NCCL windows, never through in-process peer mappings. The check postdates the kernel (added in ac4356ceb, "Skip symmetric memory tests in ragged_all_to_all_e2e_test when unsupported", vs the kernel landing without it in acb5aaffe / #41903), which suggests a CI qualifier promoted into a runtime precondition; a gate keyed on the NCCL-reported LSA domain (as the [one-shot path already does](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/7c3dd1936addd297d7c6fa46f6183986fc4160c3/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc#L1009-L1015)) seems closer to the kernel's real precondition. One caution before opening the gate: when we relaxed it that way locally, 4-host training runs produced reproducible nondeterministic all-rank NaNs while isolated/chained collective loops stayed bitwise-clean, so the [LSA branch's `memory_order_relaxed` entry barrier](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/7c3dd1936addd297d7c6fa46f6183986fc4160c3/xla/stream_executor/gpu/ragged_all_to_all_device_kernel_lib.cu.h#L199-L211) (the GIN branch uses acquire) may also need a look. Full experiment logs available on request; happy to run diagnostics on GB200 NVL72.

## Environment

GB200 NVL72 (also reproduces on any multi-GPU host, per above) · CUDA driver 13020 · NCCL 2.30.7 · jax nightly 0.11.1.dev20260809 (XLA 753e5e56a)

issue.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

Ragged EP now trains the exact four-node proxy with zero routing drops and reaches 19.63% mean MFU, up from 11.28%. Two independent problems caused the original result: XLA's latency-hiding schedule corrupted the first backward at larger expert banks, and the one-shot ragged transfer launched only one 128-thread block per peer. Disabling latency hiding and splitting each peer slice into 32 updates makes the transport finite and raises its grid from 16 to 512 blocks. Reusing the existing QuACK/CuTe SM100 grouped GEMMs removes most of the remaining local expert-compute gap.

The final command-buffer arm completed cleanly but regressed the proxy to 19.34% MFU. Exact-shape weight-gradient tile sweeps bound the remaining packaged kernel gain below the target. The selected configuration therefore remains just under 20%; a full-rack validation is the remaining production gate, not another obvious NCCL or XLA flag.

### Helpful links

- [Implementation PR #8081](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8081)
- [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/101)
- [Original XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s25-exact-ep16-e48-profile-20260810)
- [Split-32 XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s29-exact-ep16-e48-split32-profile-20260810)
- [CuTe XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s34-exact-ep16-e48-split32-cute-profile-20260810)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Experiment contract

The exact proxy used d6144/L48, 48 routed experts of width 6272, latent width 3072, top-4 routing, capacity 1.33, EP16, and 1,048,576 tokens per step across four GB200 nodes. Each node ran four one-device JAX processes. Scored jobs occupied one rack and NVLink domain. PGLE, gradient watch, eval, periodic metric steps, profiling, and checkpoints were disabled for timing runs. Results use steps 5-24.

The proxy matches the one-rack EP64 hero's per-GPU work: both route 65,536 tokens and hold three experts per GPU. EP64 raises global batch and device count together, so it does not enlarge local expert GEMMs or imply a larger-run uplift. A full-rack validation is still required before changing the hero run.

## Results

| Arm | Step time | Tokens/s | MFU | Result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| One update/peer, latency hiding on, overlap 4 | 33.7040 s | 31,112 | 11.3220% | Finite exact baseline |
| One update/peer, latency hiding off, overlap 1 | 33.8187 s | 31,006 | 11.2834% | Safe flags neutral at exact shape |
| 32 updates/peer, Pallas expert compute | 21.1090 s | 49,675 | 18.0770% | 60.21% throughput gain |
| Split-32, 4 MiB NCCL buffer | 21.1213 s | 49,647 | 18.0669% | Neutral |
| Split-32, QuACK/CuTe expert compute | 19.4429 s | 53,940 | 19.6291% | Best stable configuration |
| Split-32, CuTe, command buffers on | 19.7338 s | 53,137 | 19.3369% | 1.49% throughput regression |

Every completed exact arm had finite loss and zero dropped assignments, dropped-token fraction, or router overflow.

## Findings

- XLA latency hiding corrupts the first backward pass at larger expert banks. Disabling `--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler` restores finite training. The ragged runtime also uses collective overlap limit 1; this improved the small EP8/E96 proxy but was neutral on exact EP16/E48.
- The original ragged kernel used `grid=(16,1,1)` and consumed 13.82 seconds per step. Split-32 selects XLA's existing multi-update path, uses `grid=(16,1,32)`, and reduces the transfer to 0.78 seconds per step without changing capacity or tensor layout.
- After split-32, the gap to fixed all-to-all was expert compute. Ragged `moe_up_down` took 8.965 seconds per step versus 4.502 seconds for fixed; ragged communication was 0.886 seconds faster. The CuTe flavor keeps ragged dispatch/combine and runs the activation-path grouped GEMMs through QuACK/CuTe, reducing clean step time by another 7.89%.
- CuTe XProf measures 2.084 seconds per step in the two retained Pallas weight-gradient contractions. Exact one-GB200 sweeps covered 64/128/256 output tiles, K16/K32/K64, two/four pipeline stages, and four/eight warps. The only win was 7.54% on `dw13`; `dw2` retained its original tile. Combining the measured ceiling predicts 19.74% MFU, so it does not justify a four-node arm by itself.
- The trace already contains `ncclSymkDevKernel_AllGather_STMC`, so NCCL automatically selected its NVLS multicast path for the largest all-gathers. Forcing NVLS or SHARP cannot accelerate the custom ragged peer-write kernel. Increasing `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` from 1 MiB to 4 MiB was neutral.
- The XLA `ragged_dot_general` alternative OOMed before step zero on a single 159.32 GiB allocation. The generic symmetric put/signal backend failed with `ncclPutSignal: srcWinHost is not in a valid symmetric window`; the pinned GXL backend is unimplemented.
- Process-per-GPU needs the hero host-memory reservation. A 256 GiB four-node reservation OOM-killed a worker; 850 GiB per node completed. Auto-PGLE is not usable in this topology because four CUPTI sessions on one node collide. The separate stale retry-coordinator bug was fixed in [#8079](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8079).

## Decision

Use one process per GPU, 850 GiB of host memory per node, latency hiding disabled, collective overlap limit 1, 32 logical updates per peer, and the QuACK/CuTe ragged expert backend. Keep PGLE and periodic diagnostic work off for timing. Preserve one update per peer as the general library default and select 32 explicitly in this hero configuration until other shapes are profiled.

Keep `FUSION,CUSTOM_CALL` command buffers disabled. They completed without the historical B200 teardown failure but increased mean step time by 1.50%. Even stacking the independently measured `dw13` tile gain perfectly with that arm predicts about 19.45% MFU, so no combined four-node treatment is justified.

The conventional NCCL, transfer-splitting, packaged grouped-matmul, and bounded Pallas tile arms are exhausted for this proxy. A full one-rack EP64 run should validate the selected configuration but is not expected to improve per-GPU MFU merely through scale.

## Artifacts

- [Experiment logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/hero-run-why-can-t-we-ragged-all/.agents/logbooks/ragged-ep64.md)
- [Split-32 W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-s28-exact-ep16-e48-split32-perf-20260810)
- [CuTe W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-s33-exact-ep16-e48-split32-cute-perf-20260810)
- [Command-buffer W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-s37-exact-ep16-e48-split32-cute-command-buffers-20260810)
- Weight-gradient benchmark: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/benchmarks/ragged-weight-grad-gb200/2026.08.10.38/results.json`
- [PR #8013](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8013)
- [FSDP sweep #8054](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8054)

issue.body:
The one-shot ragged-all-to-all crashes when the clique has more than 32 devices. We see this on GB200 NVL72 (16 nodes × 4 GPUs, one 64-device clique, one process per GPU). The first execution fails on many ranks at once with `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`. The crash is deterministic (5/5 training runs). The identical program at 16 ranks runs correctly.

## Minimal repro

The repro needs more than 32 GPUs in one NVLink domain. Smaller domains (for example, B200 NVL8) never reach the affected path. Verified on GB200 NVL72 with stock nightly `0.11.1.dev20260811`: 64 devices crash, 16 devices print `ok`.

```python
# One process per GPU (or per node) across a >32-GPU NVLink domain.
#   export XLA_FLAGS='--xla_gpu_ragged_all_to_all_mode=symmetric'
#   python repro.py <coordinator_host:port> <num_processes> <process_id>
# If the one-shot declines (INVALID_ARGUMENT: "fallback to NCCL is not allowed"),
# add --xla_gpu_unsupported_override_fast_interconnect_slice_size=<total GPUs>.
import sys
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, numpy as np
from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P

coord, n_proc, pid = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3])
jax.distributed.initialize(coord, num_processes=n_proc, process_id=pid)
n = jax.device_count()
mesh = Mesh(np.array(jax.devices()), ("x",))

def f(operand, output):
    i = jax.lax.axis_index("x").astype(jnp.int64)
    in_off = jnp.arange(n, dtype=jnp.int64)       # local row j goes to peer j
    sizes = jnp.ones(n, dtype=jnp.int64)
    out_off = jnp.full((n,), i, dtype=jnp.int64)  # receiver row = sender index
    recv = jnp.ones(n, dtype=jnp.int64)
    return jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all(operand, output, in_off, sizes, out_off, recv, axis_name="x")

operand = jnp.arange(n * n * 4, dtype=jnp.bfloat16).reshape(n * n, 4)
output = jnp.zeros((n * n, 4), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)
result = jax.jit(jax.shard_map(f, mesh=mesh, in_specs=(P("x"), P("x")), out_specs=P("x")))(operand, output)
jax.block_until_ready(result)
print(f"process {jax.process_index()}: ok ({n} devices)", flush=True)
```

## Root cause hypothesis

The one-shot barrier supports at most [`kMaxPeers = 32`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/stream_executor/gpu/multi_gpu_barrier_kernel.h#L52) peers ([both kernel variants](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/stream_executor/gpu/multi_gpu_barrier_kernel.h#L69)). [`LaunchMultiGpuBarrier`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/collective_kernel_api.cc#L88) rejects larger cliques with a [`TF_RET_CHECK`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/collective_kernel_api.cc#L94-L95). The NCCL-window variant [`LaunchMultiGpuBarrierWithNccl`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/collective_kernel_api.cc#L120) has no such check. It launches with a [32-slot signal layout](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/collective_kernel_api.cc#L137) and passes `num_devices = 64` to the device kernel. Ranks then index signal slots past the 32-slot region of the symmetric window. The result is device memory corruption instead of a clean error.

The [thunk selects this path](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/3a767ceae167531faac975b92aa6d1df1a7bcedd/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc#L1008-L1015) whenever `lsa_size == num_devices`. That condition is always true for a rack-wide NVL72 clique.

## Fix validation

We rebuilt `jax-cuda13-pjrt` at the dev20260811 pins with one change: `kMaxPeers = 32 → 128`. The kernel is fully parameterized on the constant. The crash at 64 ranks is gone. A 25-step expert-parallel MoE training benchmark (384 experts, top-8 routing) completes 25/25 steps. At 16 ranks, the patched wheel matches stock throughput (22.48% vs 22.46% MFU).

## Environment

- GB200 NVL72, 16 nodes × 4 GPUs, one process per GPU, CUDA 13
- jax/jaxlib/plugin/pjrt `0.11.1.dev20260811` (stock nightly), NCCL 2.30.7
- Crash analyzed at jax `fe0f1193` / xla `3a767cea`; fix validated on a rebuild at jax `8d1be7d7` / xla `60f8069e`
- Related: [#47146](https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47146) (ragged-all-to-all device-kernel peer-access gate on the same topology)

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This campaign tested whether the ragged EP64 all-to-all path could match the fixed-transport hero throughput target while keeping trained-router drops below 2% at the full 8/384 hero shape on one NVL72 rack. The drop criterion is met with large margin: the real-LR drop-trajectory run averaged 0.107% drops over steps 250-299 at cf 1.15. Throughput improved from the initial 20.20% MFU / 223k tok/s configuration to a 21.82% MFU / 241k tok/s frontier after QuACK GEMM scheduling work, with zero drops and bit-identical loss across the tuning arms. The issue's current conclusion is that the in-scope configuration and compute-tuning levers are exhausted: split counts, store width, symmetric buffers, fused device kernel, command buffers, HBM optimizer residency, GEMM tile/cluster/persistence, backward mask removal, and overlap-limit changes do not close the remaining gap. Reaching the original ~25% / ~300k tok/s target now depends on a faster structural transport path, tracked separately in marin-ep, rather than more launch-flag tuning here.

### Helpful links
- Prior ragged EP64 crash/fix campaign: #8077
- Capacity/drop analysis: #8062
- Upstream ragged all-to-all gate: https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47283
- Configuration phase conclusion: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5305649465
- Compute-tuning frontier: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5308322722
- Final in-scope lever closure: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5309167198
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## TL;DR

Campaign start. The ragged all-to-all hero (E384, top-8, i3072, EP64 on one NVL72 rack) runs at 20.20% MFU / 223k tokens/s (`ra2a-mw-g17`, cf 1.00, LR≈0 harness). The goal is throughput comparable to the fixed-transport `moe_hero_ep` template (~25% MFU, ~300k tokens/s per rack) while holding steady-state trained-router drops under 2%.

## Description

#8077 root-caused and fixed the EP64 one-shot crash (openxla/xla#47283, kMaxPeers rebuild wheel) and validated the first ragged EP64 hero run. The ragged transport pools receiver capacity per device, so it drops far less than `fixed_all_to_all` at the same capacity factor: at cf 1.1–1.2 the trained-regime drop rate measures ≤0.05% (analytical replay of #8062 histograms; empirical r02 at EP16), versus ~4% for the fixed template at cf 1.30–1.33. What remains is a throughput gap.

Reference points at hero scale on one rack: fixed transport at iso-active-compute (`mhep-baseline-e192k4-i6144-cf133-fp32-20260814-c`) reaches 23.6% MFU / 251k tokens/s at ~3.9% drops; the half-active-compute reference (`mhep-baseline-e192k4-cf133-fp32-20260814-b`, i3072) reaches 25.3% / 346k.

Constraints: no model change, and no quantization beyond what `moe_hero_ep` on main already performs (per the [fidelity discussion](https://openathena.slack.com/archives/C0AHF5KV11Q/p1786740832465729?thread_ts=1786583521.652629&cid=C0AHF5KV11Q)). The ragged training path is currently bf16 end to end.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reach ~25% MFU / ~300k tokens/s at the full hero shape (d6144/L48, E384, top-8, i3072, latent 3072, batch 1024) on one NVL72 rack with the ragged transport, then demonstrate <2% steady-state drops at the chosen capacity posture and loss parity against the existing EP implementation via `small_scale_abl_launch.py`.

## Status

h01 (cf 1.15 posture baseline) and h02 (latency-hiding scheduler + overlap limit 4, retesting the safe-flag retreat adopted on the broken barrier generation) are running. Queued: splits-per-peer sweep at EP64, command buffers at the #8277 capture set, XProf anatomy of the best configuration.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/ragged-ep64.md` (branch `ra2a-mw/s48-diag`)
* Prior campaign: #8077
* Upstream fix: https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47283
* Capacity/drop analysis: #8062
* W&B: runs under `marin-community/marin_moe`, prefix `ra2a-mw-h*`

## Decision Log

# Marin standup — August 17th, 2026

**Previous standup**: [Week of August 3rd, 2026 standup](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8019)

**Hero run burndown issues**: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8233

## Ben Feuer ([@penfever](https://github.com/penfever))

### Last week

- 5.7T Snowball Cold Start SFT + Eval e2e -> [GH Issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8225), [Public Report](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/standing-up-a-cold-start-sft-pipeline-for-marin-models/2026.08.16/index.html), [Discord Post](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1355318637854199848/1538575722598105149)
  - Eval scores improve with continued pretraining and post-training: 89% on GSM8K 0-shot, 78% on MATH500, 38% on AIME24 for our best checkpoints
  - Agentic eval results are also strong: 20.4% for Snowball 5.7T on OT-TBLite vs 23.0% for Qwen3 8B on the same SFT data (nemotron terminal)
- Ablations on agentic RL: harness, context length, dataset, summarization: [GH Issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8361), [Public Report](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/harness-context-length-summ-ablation/2026.08.17/index.html)
  - Tl;dr this is a messy space and there’s no great answers
  - Probably we will get the cleanest signal on *data quality* if we RL on terminus-2 at 131k context length … but even this simple statement needs like 8 qualifiers
  - If you have an appetite for it the public report goes into lots of detail
- Had fun seeing everyone in SF last week!

### This week

- Post training futuresight
  - I want to understand from people how we can better communicate about our post-training roadmap; the what, the why, and how people can help
